title: Alkalinity Boost Changes Algae Growth and Lipids
dek: A 16‑day study shows that raising seawater alkalinity alters Isochrysis galbana’s growth, stress enzymes, and lipid metabolism, indicating a shift from growth to defense.
body: Researchers simulated two levels of ocean alkalinity enhancement (+600 and +1200 µmol kg⁻¹ total alkalinity) and monitored the nanophytoplankton Isochrysis galbana for 16 days. They confirmed that the carbonate chemistry of the water matched the intended alkalinity gradients. During the early part of the experiment, the algae grew normally, showing physiological resilience to the higher alkalinity. Toward the later stages, growth slowed and antioxidant enzyme activities rose modestly, suggesting the cells were beginning to experience stress. Metabolite and transcript analyses revealed extensive reprogramming of the algae’s internal chemistry. Energy‑storage compounds and lipid profiles changed markedly, reflecting a shift of resources from growth and storage toward defensive functions. These observations highlight that while short‑term exposure to increased alkalinity may be tolerated, longer exposure can suppress growth and remodel lipid metabolism, important considerations for evaluating the ecological safety of ocean alkalinity enhancement.
why: Understanding how key microalgae adjust to alkalinity changes helps assess risks and guide safe use of ocean alkalinity enhancement in climate mitigation.

title: Bubbleless CO₂ membrane aeration boosts algae growth and nutrient removal from urine
dek: Delivering CO₂ through a membrane raises Chlorella vulgaris biomass and sharply improves nitrogen and phosphorus capture from source‑separated urine.
body: Researchers tested a bubbleless CO₂ membrane aeration method while growing the microalga Chlorella vulgaris in both fresh and hydrolyzed urine. By supplying inorganic carbon directly through the membrane, they could control how much CO₂ the algae received. With this controlled CO₂ delivery, the algae produced 25 % more biomass compared with conventional cultivation. At the same time, the system removed 28 % more total nitrogen and more than double the phosphorus (112 % increase) from the urine. Molecular analyses showed that the membrane‑mediated CO₂ supply turned on genes linked to carbon fixation (acsA, acsE) and nitrogen assimilation (ureC, gdhA). The fresh urine plus CO₂ condition displayed a strong coupling of carbon and nitrogen metabolism, meaning that balanced carbon availability and the gradual release of nitrogen worked together to enhance photosynthesis and nutrient uptake. The study concludes that the benefit of bubbleless CO₂ membrane aeration goes beyond simply adding carbon; it also improves the internal coordination of carbon and nitrogen pathways, offering a clearer mechanistic basis for algae‑based wastewater treatment that recovers resources while fixing carbon.
why: Understanding how CO₂ delivery coordinates carbon‑nitrogen metabolism helps design algae systems that turn urine waste into valuable biomass and recover nutrients efficiently.

title: Copepod Diets Reveal Dinoflagellate Dominance in Subarctic Pacific
dek: Isotope analysis shows Calanus spp. rely heavily on dinoflagellates in the Bering Strait, while tropical diets include more nitrogen‑fixers and bacteria.
body: Researchers examined the stomach contents of the widespread copepod Calanus spp. across the western North Pacific by measuring carbon and nitrogen isotope ratios in amino acids. These chemical fingerprints let them estimate which groups of organisms formed the base of the copepods' diet. In tropical and subtropical waters, the copepods' diet was composed of about 20% nitrogen‑fixing organisms and roughly 30% heterotrophic bacteria. By contrast, in the Bering Strait and southern Chukchi Sea, more than half of the diet (around 54%) came from dinoflagellates, a type of phytoplankton. The study also linked nitrogen sources to region: tropical phytoplankton primarily used biologically fixed nitrogen, while in the Pacific Arctic Ocean, nitrate supplied over 90% of the nitrogen taken up by eukaryotic microalgae. These patterns suggest that regional nutrient changes are reshaping plankton food webs.
why: Understanding which microalgae feed key zooplankton helps predict how climate‑driven nutrient changes will impact marine food chains and biotechnological harvesting of algae.

title: Nannochloropsis strains produce high‑quality biodiesel
dek: Three Nannochloropsis species were grown under nitrogen‑starved, high‑light conditions, yielding up to 143 mg L⁻¹ day⁻¹ lipid and >98% conversion to biodiesel that meets ASTM and EN standards.
body: Researchers cultivated three Nannochloropsis species—N. oceanica (IMET1), N. granulata and N. limnetica—in a 20‑L bubble‑column photobioreactor using a nitrogen‑deficient, high‑light BG‑11 medium to encourage lipid accumulation. After harvesting, lipids were extracted with hexane in an automated Soxhlet system and profiled by high‑resolution GC‑MS. The extracted oils underwent supercritical methanol transesterification, producing methyl esters with yields of 98.74 % for N. oceanica, 98.35 % for N. granulata and 96.12 % for N. limnetica. Fuel properties were measured according to ASTM D6751 and EN 14214, and all three biodiesels satisfied these quality standards. N. oceanica showed the highest lipid productivity (142.9 ± 3.42 mg L⁻¹ day⁻¹) and oil content (57.5 % dry weight), as well as an especially high cetane number (57.63) and calorific value (41.85 MJ kg⁻¹), indicating strong ignition performance and potential fuel‑efficiency benefits.
why: Demonstrating efficient, high‑quality biodiesel from Nannochloropsis supports scalable microalgae routes to renewable fuels.

title: Plasma‑treated chitosan dressing powers algae to heal diabetic wounds
dek: A cold atmospheric plasma‑modified chitosan matrix couples red‑light‑activated microalgae to boost oxygen and energy production, speeding closure of diabetic skin wounds.
body: Researchers created a wound dressing by treating chitosan, a sugar‑based polymer, with cold atmospheric plasma and then embedding the microalga *Chlamydomonas* (CHL). The plasma reshapes the polymer in a time‑dependent way, with a 30‑second treatment giving the most favorable structure for linking the algae. When the dressing is illuminated with 660 nm red light, the algae perform photosynthesis within the polymer matrix. At the optimal plasma condition, the system shows the lowest oxygen‑quenching index (about 66 %), indicating more available O₂, and it also increases hydrogen output and photosynthetic electron flow by roughly 115‑120 % compared with untreated material. In a streptozotocin‑induced diabetic mouse model, wounds covered with the plasma‑engineered chitosan‑algae dressing and exposed to red light closed faster than wounds with no dressing or with plain chitosan. Blood counts remained normal. Tissue analysis revealed reduced inflammation, more blood‑vessel formation, lower reactive‑oxygen species, restored mitochondrial function, and activation of cellular recycling pathways. The study shows that fine‑tuning carbohydrate polymers with plasma can program microalgal photobioenergetics, turning a simple dressing into a light‑driven bio‑factory that supports diabetic wound repair.
why: Programming microalgal photosynthesis within a polymer dressing offers a scalable, light‑controlled way to deliver bioenergy and regenerative cues for diabetic wound therapies.

title: Humic acids and salts reshape nanoplastic toxicity to algae
dek: Combined humic acid and cations alter nanoplastic aggregation, bioaccessibility, and toxicity pathways in Chlorella vulgaris.
body: Researchers examined how polystyrene nanoplastics interact with the freshwater alga Chlorella vulgaris under three water‑chemistry conditions: humic acid alone, sodium or calcium ions alone, and a mixture of humic acid with those cations. They found that when humic acid and cations were present together, the nanoplastics formed larger aggregates with the algae and became more bioavailable, yet the algae showed less growth inhibition than with cations alone. This reduced toxicity was linked to lower membrane damage, less disruption of photosynthesis, and fewer signs of programmed cell death. In contrast, compared with humic acid alone, the humic‑cation mixture increased nanoplastic bioaccessibility, raised oxidative stress, and caused greater membrane destabilization, leading to higher overall toxicity. Quantitative analysis showed bioaccessibility rising from about 1.1 µg per 10⁴ cells to over 3 µg per 10⁴ cells when both humic acid and cations were present. Statistical modeling indicated that increased bioaccessibility drives toxicity only when it coincides with oxidative stress and membrane damage, revealing a conditional cascade of effects. These results demonstrate that the combined presence of natural organic matter and common ions can fundamentally change how nanoplastics affect algae, a nuance that single‑factor experiments miss. The authors suggest that realistic water‑chemistry scenarios should be included in risk assessments for nanoplastics in freshwater ecosystems.
why: Understanding how natural organic matter and ions together modify nanoplastic impacts helps build more accurate safety guidelines for freshwater algal cultures used in biotech.

title: Photosynthetic Biofilm Carriers Boost Wastewater Treatment and Biomass Yield
dek: A systematic review finds that carrier type matters less than operating conditions for efficient nutrient removal and algae biomass production.
body: Researchers examined many studies of photosynthetic biofilm reactors that use carriers to grow algae on surfaces instead of in suspension. By categorising the data on carrier biodegradability and applying multivariate analysis, they identified which factors most affect performance. The analysis showed that reactor orientation—whether horizontal, vertical, inclined, or rotating—did not significantly change treatment outcomes. Instead, operational parameters such as light exposure and the area available for growth were the main drivers of biomass yield, explaining about 80% of the variation. Across the reviewed systems, average removal efficiencies were 82% for chemical oxygen demand, 78% for total nitrogen, and 88% for total phosphate. Typical operating conditions worldwide included a pH around 7.8, 14 hours of light per day, a 9‑day hydraulic retention time, and a temperature near 26 °C. These findings suggest that selecting reactor designs that can maintain optimal light and surface area will be more important than the specific carrier material, guiding future scale‑up of algal biofilm technologies for wastewater treatment and bio‑product generation.
why: Understanding the key drivers of biofilm reactor performance helps design more efficient microalgae systems for clean water and renewable biomass.
